overview: The map’s 1920 to 1938 record is labelled with Tanzania’s later name. At that time the mainland territory was Tanganyika, administered by Britain under a League of Nations mandate. Tanzania’s union with Zanzibar came only in 1964. This card follows Tanganyika’s interwar farmers, readers, workers and colonial institutions.

periods.title: British administration after German rule
periods.summary: The postwar territorial settlement led to a British mandate confirmed in 1922.

periods.title: Mandate-era life
periods.summary: Coffee growers, sisal production and Swahili newspapers connected local work to wider markets and politics.

periods.title: Beyond this map interval
periods.summary: Tanganyika became independent in 1961 and joined Zanzibar in 1964.

items.text: On Kilimanjaro, African smallholders grew coffee alongside European settlers. Colonial encouragement of local growers provoked settler opposition. Coffee history therefore includes a contest over who could farm and sell, as well as the plants themselves.

The Kilimanjaro Native Planters Association brought growers into organized politics. Cooperative legislation in 1932 and coffee controls in 1937 shaped how crops reached markets. An association and its paperwork could matter to a farming household as much as a harvest.

Sisal production expanded rapidly in Tanganyika and Kenya during the 1920s and 1930s. The Depression brought low prices and unstable markets, creating conflict between producers and merchants. More output did not automatically mean a more secure income.

Economic historian Sascha Klocke identifies restricted educational opportunities for Africans as a major barrier to advancement in paid employment. The supply of trained workers helped determine who obtained skilled jobs and higher wages.

Klocke’s study also separates racial discrimination from shortages of trained personnel. These interacted: importing skilled workers could widen income differences while inadequate African education helped preserve the shortage. Colonial wage inequality cannot be explained by one pay rule alone.

“Mambo Leo” means “Affairs of Today”. This attested Swahili title belonged to a monthly launched by the Education Department in January 1923. It is a small original-language sample of the printed material circulating during this map period.

Mambo Leo printed entertaining stories, arranged pen friendships and carried notices looking for missing people. A newspaper could help someone find a correspondent or reconnect with a person, alongside passing on official news.

The paper’s early topics included agriculture, education, veterinary matters and football. Its staff selected news according to government policy, including support for Swahili in primary schools. Useful reading and colonial persuasion occupied the same printed pages.

In Ulanga, river communities used canoes for transport and combined fishing with other work. The Kilombero floodplain offered fertile land, but seasonal floods interrupted routes and separated places. Water was both a resource and a practical constraint.

Food production varied with local conditions: rice grew in lowlands and uplands, while farmers also cultivated maize and sorghum with hoes. Pogoro near the floodplain grew more rice than highland Pogoro. A community name alone does not tell us what was for dinner.

During the 1930s, colonial officials debated moving scattered communities into concentrated settlements as a response to sleeping sickness. In Ulanga, proposals preceded the outbreak recorded in 1939. Medical goals became entangled with power over where families could live.

Tanganyika’s 1961 constitution marked a later political transformation beyond the map’s interwar interval. Independence changed sovereignty; the people who had farmed, read newspapers and worked under colonial rule did not disappear when the legal framework changed.

ending.text: British rule ended with Tanganyika’s independence on 9 December 1961. Tanganyika joined Zanzibar on 26 April 1964 to form the union later named Tanzania. This imported interwar record should not be read as evidence that the United Republic already existed in the 1920s.
